sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: Viewers post comments on a live video. Other viewers receive them quickly. Stored history supports later joins and reconnects.
A comment is small, but one comment can have millions of recipients. Distribution creates the main scaling challenge.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: A viewer can post a comment on a live video.
A viewer can receive new comments and request comments posted before joining.
After a connection failure, the viewer can recover a bounded set of missed comments.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: The target is less than 200 ms for typical live delivery. The scenario includes millions of viewers and high comment rates.
Favor availability over immediate consistency. Persist accepted comments and recover from connection-server failures.
Define comment ordering within each video. Replayed events must not appear twice in the viewer's feed.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: User identifies a commenter, viewer, or broadcaster. Live Video identifies the stream and its comment channel.
Comment contains its ID, video ID, author, text, and creation time. An ordering key supports history queries.
A subscription connects a viewer's active connection to a video. Each messaging server keeps its local subscriptions.
A cursor records the last applied comment position. It supports pagination and recovery after a disconnect.

sections.title: API
points: POST /comments/{liveVideoId} creates a comment. The server obtains the user ID from the validated session token.
GET /comments/{liveVideoId} returns a bounded history page. A cursor and page size identify the requested range.
An SSE connection receives new comments. HTTP requests can still submit comments. WebSockets provide an alternative transport.
Responses include comment IDs and ordering information. These let the client merge history and live events without duplicates.

sections.title: 1) Post and store comments
points: The Comment Management Service validates the request. It stores the comment in the Comments DB, using DynamoDB in the source design.
Live publication is added later. A reliable publication record or outbox can prevent a gap after database commit.
Organize history by video ID and ordering key. Use a consistent key schema for both writes and range queries.

flows.title: Store a comment
steps: The Commenter Client sends a comment and video ID to the Comment Management Service.
The service validates the request and obtains the author from the session.
The service writes the comment to the Comments DB. It confirms acceptance after storage succeeds.

sections.title: 2) Deliver and read history
points: The initial design polls the Comment Management Service for comments after the last received position. This creates many empty reads.
Historical pages use a cursor to request older comments. Offset pagination can skip or repeat comments when the feed changes.
The later push design must coordinate history with live events. Buffer events or use a shared boundary during the transition.

flows.title: Poll for new comments
steps: The Viewer Client sends the last received comment position to the server.
The Comment Management Service queries the database for later comments on that video.
The server returns the new comments. The client displays them and advances its cursor.
The client repeats the request after a polling interval. This initial design trades delivery delay against request volume.

sections.title: 1) Real-time transport
points: Polling is simple, but frequent requests increase load. Infrequent requests increase delivery delay.
SSE supports server-to-client updates over one open connection. The source uses HTTP POST for comment creation.
WebSockets support communication in both directions. Choose them when the interaction requires that capability.
Check proxy buffering, connection limits, and heartbeats. Neither transport supplies durable history by itself.

flows.title: Push comments through SSE
steps: The viewer opens an SSE connection and selects a video.
The Comment Management Service stores a newly submitted comment in the database.
The service sends the stored comment to its connected viewers for that video.
Each client deduplicates the comment ID and adds the comment to its feed.

sections.title: 2) Audience fanout
points: A single Redis Pub/Sub channel sends every comment to every messaging server. This wastes work on irrelevant videos.
Partition channels by video ID. Each Realtime Messaging Server subscribes only to channels needed by its viewers.
A Layer 7 Load Balancer can place viewers of the same video on related servers. This reduces unnecessary subscriptions.
A Dispatcher is an alternative to pub/sub. It looks up the responsible servers and sends each comment directly to them.
Keep routing and subscription state current as servers join or fail. ZooKeeper or etcd can hold shared coordination data.
A viral video can exceed one server's capacity. Distribute its viewers across servers and bound buffers for slow clients.
Redis Pub/Sub does not retain missed events. Recover missed live comments from stored history or a shared recent-history cache.

flows.title: Route comments with partitioned pub-sub
steps: The Layer 7 Load Balancer routes a viewer using the video ID.
The Realtime Messaging Server records the connection. It subscribes to the Redis Pub/Sub channels needed by its viewers.
The Comment Management Service stores a new comment. It publishes the comment to the video's assigned channel.
Interested messaging servers receive the event. Each server sends it to the relevant local SSE connections.
Servers update subscriptions when their viewer population changes. Stored history supplies missed comments after a failure.

flows.title: Route comments with a dispatcher
steps: A messaging server registers the videos watched by its connected viewers.
The Comment Management Service stores a new comment and sends it to the Dispatcher.
The Dispatcher looks up the messaging servers responsible for that video. It forwards the comment to those servers.
Each messaging server sends the comment to its local viewers through SSE.

sections.title: 3) Reconnection and overload
points: On reconnect, send the last applied comment ID. Request later comments before continuing normal live delivery.
Deduplicate overlapping history and live events by comment ID. Use ordering information to merge them consistently.
Limit replay duration and result size. For a long absence, show a recent snapshot and allow the viewer to jump to live.
For extreme traffic, sample comments or serve a recent-comment snapshot through a CDN. This changes the delivery target and completeness.
The source's CDN alternative permits about one to two seconds of delay. The client can display its own comment immediately.
Use different thresholds to enter and leave snapshot mode. Heartbeats and delayed reconnect attempts reduce repeated connection failures.

flows.title: Recover missed comments
steps: The client records the last applied comment ID before a disconnect.
On reconnect, it sends that position through Last-Event-ID or an HTTP catch-up request.
The server returns a bounded set of later comments from shared history. The client buffers concurrent live events during recovery.
The client merges history and live events by their ordering keys. It removes duplicate comment IDs.
The client advances its cursor after applying each event. If replay is unavailable, it shows a recent snapshot and the gap.

sections.title: Final Design
points: The Comment Management Service stores comments in DynamoDB. The final source diagram uses a Dispatcher to locate interested messaging servers.
The Realtime Messaging Service sends comments through SSE. Partitioned pub/sub is a separate alternative described in the deep dive.
Cursor recovery, deduplication, bounded replay, and special handling for viral videos keep the viewing experience usable at scale.
